items.en: Two Schemes: Against the Foundations of Mindfulness
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明觀門制立不同 · 對四念處
parent: The Sixteen Special Excellences: Their Name

zh: 第二、明觀門制立不同者，解有二：一者、有人云：「此阿那波那等十六法對四念處。」若約四念處而明，當知但在欲界、未到地乃至初禪則具足也，欲至上地，非為不得，但觀法式少不具足。如四禪，既無出入息及喜、樂等，若約息及喜、樂明念處，則不便也。上下類而可知。亦明對四念處，復有二解不同：一師解云：「前五對身，中三對受，次二對心，後五對法。」
en: Second, clarifying the differing schemes for establishing the contemplation-gates: there are two interpretations. First, some say: "This method of mindfulness of the breath and the other sixteen dharmas correspond to the four foundations of mindfulness." Discussed with reference to the four foundations of mindfulness, one should know that this is complete only within the desire realm, the "not-yet-arrived" state, and the first dhyāna; wishing to reach the higher stages, it is not that this cannot be attained there, only that the manner of contemplation is somewhat incomplete. As in the fourth dhyāna, which has no in-breath or out-breath, nor joy or happiness present at all — were the foundations of mindfulness to be explained with reference to the breath, joy, and happiness specifically, this would not fit properly there. The stages above and below may be understood by the same pattern.

Also, in explaining their correspondence to the four foundations of mindfulness, there are, in turn, two differing interpretations. One master explains: "The first five correspond to the body; the middle three correspond to sensation; the next two correspond to mind; and the last five correspond to dharma."

zh: 此師明十六特勝。自云依《禪經》中說：一、觀入息，至於氣滅。二、觀出息，止至於鼻端。三、觀息長短，若身不安，心多散亂，則出入息俱短；若身安心靜，則出入息俱長。四、息遍身者，形心既安，則氣道無壅，如似飲氣，既統遍身中。五、除諸身行者，想、受為心行，覺觀為口行，出入息為身行。既息遍身中，患彼覺動麁念，除諸麁故，名除諸身行。此五屬身念處。
en: This master clarifies the sixteen special excellences, stating that this follows what the Dhyāna Sūtra itself says: first, observing the in-breath, all the way to the breath's own cessation. Second, observing the out-breath, stopping right at the tip of the nose. Third, observing the breath's length and shortness: if the body is not at ease, the mind for the most part scattered and disordered, both the in-breath and out-breath are short; if the body is at ease and the mind still, both the in-breath and out-breath are long. Fourth, the breath pervading the whole body: once form and mind are at ease, the channel of the breath's own energy is no longer obstructed, as though drinking in the breath, its flow now governing the entire body throughout. Fifth, removing every bodily formation: conception and sensation are mental formations; initial thought and sustained reflection are verbal formations; and the in-breath and out-breath are bodily formations. Once the breath pervades the whole body, one becomes troubled by the coarse thought stirred by initial thought's own movement, and, removing this coarseness, this is named removing every bodily formation. These first five belong to the foundation of mindfulness of the body.

zh: 受念處有三，謂麁息除故，身心安隱故。六、受喜；七、受樂者，雖有微喜，樂能遍滿身識，既滿，內心喜悅，故名樂；八、受諸心行者，既受樂在懷，必有數法相隨，倚心樂境，故名受諸心行。心念處有三：九、心作喜者，既止心一境，未有慧解，必為沈心所覆沒，以喜舉之，令不沈沒，故名作喜；十、心作攝者，喜心動散，則發越過，常攝之令還，不使馳散諸緣，故作攝；十一、心作解脫者，心不掉散，均等無累，故名解脫。
en: The foundation of mindfulness of sensation has three, since the coarse breath has now been removed, body and mind at peace. Sixth, receiving joy; seventh, receiving happiness: though there is only a faint joy present, happiness is able to fill the bodily consciousness completely, and, once full, the inward mind delights in it — hence it is named happiness. Eighth, receiving every mental formation: happiness now held within the mind, various mental factors are bound to accompany it in turn, the mind leaning upon this pleasant object — hence it is named receiving every mental formation.

The foundation of mindfulness of mind has three. Ninth, the mind making joy: the mind now stilled upon a single object, but not yet possessing wisdom's own understanding, is bound to be overwhelmed and submerged by a sinking mind — raising it up with joy keeps it from sinking; hence this is named making joy. Tenth, the mind making restraint: a mind of joy, once stirred and scattered, tends to leap and overshoot its own bounds — constantly restraining it, bringing it back, not letting it run off and scatter after various objects — hence this is named making restraint. Eleventh, the mind making liberation: the mind, no longer agitated or scattered, evenly balanced and free of entanglement — hence this is named liberation.

zh: 法念處有五：十二、觀無常者，已得自在，不為沈浮所敗，故能觀諸法無常，念念生滅，不可樂也；十三、觀散壞者，此身不久當散壞，磨滅之法，非真實有；十四、觀離欲者，此身唯是苦本，心欲離之，故名離欲；十五、觀滅者，是心住滅，多諸過患，不欲住故；十六、觀棄捨者，觀此諸法皆是過患，故名棄捨。此阿那波那等十六行是慧性，無一息入出而不覺，故彼師自云：「依經明十六特勝。」今既未見經文，但述而不作，亦未敢治定。
en: The foundation of mindfulness of dharma has five. Twelfth, contemplating impermanence: having now attained freedom, no longer defeated by either sinking or floating, one is thereby able to contemplate that all dharmas are impermanent, arising and ceasing moment to moment, nothing in them worth delighting in. Thirteenth, contemplating dispersal and decay: this very body will, before long, disperse and decay — a dharma of dissolution, without any true, real existence. Fourteenth, contemplating freedom from desire: this body is nothing but the very root of suffering, and the mind wishes to be free of it — hence this is named freedom from desire. Fifteenth, contemplating cessation: this mind abiding in cessation has many faults and troubles, and so one no longer wishes to abide in it. Sixteenth, contemplating relinquishment: contemplating that all these dharmas are themselves nothing but fault and trouble — hence this is named relinquishment.

This mindfulness of the breath and the other sixteen practices are of the nature of wisdom, with not a single breath entering or leaving that is not fully perceived — hence this master states, of his own accord, that this follows what the sūtra itself clarifies as the sixteen special excellences. Since the actual sūtra text itself has not been seen here, this is only related, not independently composed, and so it is not yet asserted here as settled and fixed.

items.en: The Second Master's Correction, and the Vertical Scheme
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明觀門制立不同 · 竪對諸禪
parent: The Sixteen Special Excellences: Their Name

zh: 次師別解云：「若對四念處起十六行，無往不爾。」但分之不調，如無漏十六行，約四諦中，一諦下有四，四四十六，有漏亦復應爾。然約四念處中說一念中有四，四四十六，義亦然。向言身念處有四，以除身行屬身者，此義不然。何以故？若心息為身行者，如《大集經》說：「息乃通於三行，非止屬身行。」今正明身行者，如《摩訶衍》說：「行名身業。」今明善惡諸業皆從心生。身息是無知之法，不能造善惡，但為行作緣。今身以心來受身，令身有所造作，名為身。今明行破於受心，即是破行也。故知此屬受念處，當知受中亦具四法也。
en: The next master gives a different explanation: "If the sixteen practices are matched against the four foundations of mindfulness, this must hold true throughout without exception" — but the division just given does not properly balance. Just as the sixteen uncontaminated practices, discussed with reference to the Four Noble Truths, have four beneath each single truth, four times four making sixteen, the contaminated version ought properly to follow the same pattern. And, discussed with reference to the four foundations of mindfulness, it should likewise be said that each single foundation of mindfulness contains four, four times four making sixteen — the same sense holding here as well.

As for the claim just given, that the foundation of mindfulness of the body has four items, with "removing bodily formations" belonging to the body: this sense does not hold. Why is this? If mind and breath together were "bodily formation," then, as the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "The breath in fact extends through all three kinds of formation, not belonging solely to bodily formation." What is properly meant by "bodily formation" is, rather, as the Mahāyāna treatise says: "'Formation' means bodily karma." Here, it is clarified that every wholesome or unwholesome karmic action whatsoever arises from the mind. The body and the breath are themselves an unknowing dharma, unable to create anything wholesome or unwholesome on their own — they serve only as the condition through which formation acts. Here, it is the body, taken up by the mind and thereby received as a body, that causes the body to have anything actually done through it at all — this is what is properly named "body." What is clarified here as "formation," then, breaks through the very mind that receives — this is precisely what is meant by breaking through formation. Hence it is known that this properly belongs to the foundation of mindfulness of sensation instead — one should know that sensation, too, is thereby complete with its own four items.

zh: 向言法中有五，觀無常屬法念處者，此亦不然。何以故？經中皆說「觀心無常，觀法無我」，今明觀無常，正是心念處也。此則一中各說有四，四四十六，於義為便也。次第二師云：「此十六法應須竪對諸禪，八觀法相關故。」所以者何？一、知息入；二、知息出者，此則對於數息；三、知息長短者，對欲界定；四、知息遍身者，對未到地定；五、除諸身行者，對初覺支；六、受喜，對初禪喜支；七、心受樂，對初禪樂支；八、受諸心行者，對初禪一心支；九、心作喜，對二禪內淨喜支；十、心作攝，對二禪一心支；十一、心住解脫，對三禪樂支；十二、觀無常，對四禪不動定；十三、觀出散，對空處；十四、觀離欲，對識處；十五、觀滅，對不用處；十六、觀棄捨，對非想非非想處。此則從初調心乃至發諸禪定明觀行具足，此解為勝也。
en: As for the claim just given, that the dharma-category has five items, with "contemplating impermanence" belonging to the foundation of mindfulness of dharma: this, too, does not hold. Why is this? The sūtras all uniformly say: "contemplate mind as impermanent, contemplate dharmas as without self" — what is clarified here as "contemplating impermanence," then, properly belongs to the foundation of mindfulness of mind instead. This, then, gives each of the four foundations its own four items, four times four, which is more convenient in its own sense.

The second master, next, says: "These sixteen dharmas should properly correspond vertically to the various dhyānas in sequence, since the eight contemplation-dharmas are mutually related to them." Why is this?

First, knowing the breath entering; second, knowing the breath leaving — these correspond to counting the breath. Third, knowing the breath's length and shortness — this corresponds to desire-realm concentration. Fourth, knowing the breath pervading the whole body — this corresponds to the "not-yet-arrived" concentration. Fifth, removing every bodily formation — this corresponds to the first dhyāna's own factor of initial thought. Sixth, receiving joy — this corresponds to the first dhyāna's own factor of joy. Seventh, the mind receiving happiness — this corresponds to the first dhyāna's own factor of happiness. Eighth, receiving every mental formation — this corresponds to the first dhyāna's own factor of one-pointedness of mind. Ninth, the mind making joy — this corresponds to the second dhyāna's own factor of inner-purity joy. Tenth, the mind making restraint — this corresponds to the second dhyāna's own factor of one-pointedness of mind. Eleventh, the mind abiding in liberation — this corresponds to the third dhyāna's own factor of happiness. Twelfth, contemplating impermanence — this corresponds to the fourth dhyāna's own unmoving concentration. Thirteenth, contemplating dispersal — this corresponds to the sphere of space. Fourteenth, contemplating freedom from desire — this corresponds to the sphere of consciousness. Fifteenth, contemplating cessation — this corresponds to the sphere of nothingness. Sixteenth, contemplating relinquishment — this corresponds to the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception.

This scheme, then, runs from the very outset of regulating the mind all the way through bringing forth every dhyāna-concentration, its own contemplative practice complete throughout — this interpretation is the superior one.

The first master's scheme sorts the sixteen items by which of the four foundations of mindfulness (body, sensation, mind, dharma) each belongs to; the next master keeps the same four-foundation axis but re-sorts two of the items; and a further, second master then proposes an entirely different organizing axis — mapping each item directly onto a specific stage of concentration, from counting the breath through the summit of the formless attainments. The treatise's own preference for the second, "vertical" scheme is significant: it turns the sixteen special excellences into a single continuous itinerary through every prior stage this whole treatise has covered — a compressed retrospective of fascicles 5 and 6 that will now be walked back through once more, this time with contemplative wisdom attached at every step rather than concentration alone.

quiz.q: If the sixteen are explained by the foundations of mindfulness, why are they complete only up to the first dhyāna?
options: the fourth dhyāna has no breath, joy, or happiness, so explaining mindfulness by them does not fit there
quiz.why: In the higher stages it is not impossible, only incomplete: the fourth dhyāna has no breath, joy, or happiness, so explaining the foundations by them does not fit.

quiz.q: How does the first master match the sixteen to the four foundations of mindfulness?
options: the first five to body, the middle three to sensation, the next two to mind, the last five to dharma
quiz.why: The first master assigns the first five to body, the middle three to sensation, the next two to mind, and the last five to dharma. Four each is the next master's view.

quiz.q: Which scripture does the first master claim, and what is Zhiyi's attitude?
options: he claims the Chan Sūtra; Zhiyi, not having seen the text, only relates it without settling it
quiz.why: The master says he follows the Chan Sūtra; Zhiyi, not having seen the text, merely relates it and does not assert it as settled.

quiz.q: In the first master's account, when are the breaths short and when long?
options: body uneasy and mind scattered: both short; body at ease and mind still: both long
quiz.why: If the body is uneasy and the mind scattered, both breaths are short; if the body is at ease and the mind still, both are long. Option B belongs to the vertical scheme in §12.

quiz.q: In the first master's account of removing bodily formation, how are the three formations distinguished?
options: conception and sensation are mental formations; initial thought and reflection verbal; breath bodily
quiz.why: Conception and sensation are mental formations, initial thought and reflection verbal formations, and the breath bodily formation. The next master later disputes this.

quiz.q: Why, in the first master's account, does the mind "make joy"?
options: stilled on one object without wisdom, it would be submerged by sinking, so joy raises it
quiz.why: The mind fixed on one object without wisdom tends to be overwhelmed by sinking, and joy lifts it.

quiz.q: What is restrained in "the mind making restraint"?
options: joy that stirs and overshoots, brought back so it does not run after objects
quiz.why: Joy, once stirred, tends to overshoot, so it is constantly restrained and brought back.

quiz.q: In the first master's account, what does "contemplating dispersal and decay" contemplate?
options: leaving the form realm and dispersing three kinds of form
this body will soon disperse and decay, a dharma of dissolution, not truly existent
quiz.why: The body will soon disperse and decay, a dharma of dissolution. Option B is the vertical scheme's explanation in §17.

quiz.q: How does the first master explain contemplating freedom from desire and contemplating relinquishment?
options: freedom from desire: the body is the root of suffering and the mind wishes to leave it; relinquishment: all these dharmas are faults
quiz.why: Freedom from desire: the body is the root of suffering and the mind wishes to be free of it; relinquishment: all these dharmas are faults. B is the vertical scheme's account.

quiz.q: How does the next master think the sixteen should be divided, and by what analogy?
options: four under each foundation, like the sixteen uncontaminated aspects with four under each truth
quiz.why: Just as the sixteen uncontaminated aspects have four under each truth, each foundation of mindfulness should have four, making sixteen.

quiz.q: Opposing the view that removing bodily formation belongs to the body, which sūtra does the next master cite on the breath extending through all three formations?
quiz.why: As the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says, the breath extends through all three kinds of formation, not only bodily formation.

quiz.q: Why does the next master assign removing bodily formation to the foundation of sensation?
options: body and breath are unknowing and create nothing; formation breaks through the receiving mind, so it belongs to sensation
quiz.why: Body and breath are unknowing and cannot create good or evil, serving only as a condition; formation breaks through the receiving mind, so it belongs to sensation, giving sensation four items.

quiz.q: Why does the next master assign contemplating impermanence to the foundation of mind?
options: the sūtras say "contemplate mind as impermanent, dharmas as without self"
quiz.why: The sūtras say to contemplate mind as impermanent and dharmas as without self, so contemplating impermanence belongs to mind, giving four to each.

quiz.q: What does the second master propose, and how does the text judge it?
options: match them vertically to the dhyānas, from regulating the mind to every concentration; this interpretation is superior
all to the first dhyāna, rejected
quiz.why: The second master matches the sixteen vertically to the dhyānas, covering everything from regulating the mind to every concentration; the text calls this superior and follows it from §11.

quiz.q: In the vertical scheme, what do items one through four correspond to?
options: breath in and out: counting; length: desire-realm concentration; pervading: not-yet-arrived
quiz.why: Knowing the breath entering and leaving corresponds to counting; length to desire-realm concentration; pervading the body to the not-yet-arrived concentration.

quiz.q: Items five through eight correspond to which factors of the first dhyāna?
options: removing bodily formation: initial thought; joy: joy; happiness: happiness; mental formations: one-pointedness
quiz.why: Removing bodily formation corresponds to initial thought, joy to joy, happiness to happiness, and every mental formation to one-pointedness.

quiz.q: What do items nine through eleven correspond to?
options: making joy: second dhyāna's inner-purity joy; restraint: its one-pointedness; liberation: third dhyāna's happiness
quiz.why: Making joy corresponds to the second dhyāna's inner-purity joy, restraint to its one-pointedness, and abiding in liberation to the third dhyāna's happiness.

quiz.q: What does contemplating impermanence correspond to vertically?
quiz.why: Contemplating impermanence corresponds to the fourth dhyāna's unmoving concentration, which ordinary people tend to take as permanent.

quiz.q: The last four correspond to the formless spheres. Which pairing is correct?
options: dispersal: space; freedom from desire: consciousness; cessation: nothingness; relinquishment: neither perception nor non-perception
quiz.why: Dispersal corresponds to the sphere of space, freedom from desire to consciousness, cessation to nothingness, and relinquishment to neither perception nor non-perception.
